en: Sutta Nipāta 1.12 Munisutta From intimacy fear is born;
Dust arises from having a home;
for one who is homeless and free from attachment—
this indeed is the vision of a sage.
He who, having cut down what has grown, would not plant again,
and would not provide for what is growing—
him they call a solitary sage wandering alone.
The Great Seer beheld the state of peace.
Having scrutinized the foundations and discarded the seed,
he would not bestow upon him any affection.
He is indeed a sage who sees the end of birth;
having abandoned reasoning, he no longer enters into worldly reckoning.
Having fully understood all attachments, he does not enter into them again.
Not desiring even one of those things,
that sage is indeed free from attachment and greed;
having gone to the further shore, he does not strive for them.
To the All-Conqueror, the All-Knowing, the Wise One,
unstained by any phenomena,
who has abandoned everything and is liberated through the destruction of craving—
The wise ones, the sages, know that too:
one endowed with the power of wisdom and possessed of virtue and conduct,
concentrated, delighting in meditation, and mindful.
The wise call him a sage who is free from attachments, unblemished, and taintless;
they call him a sage who wanders alone and remains vigilant.
Unshaken by blame or praise,
not trembling at sounds like a lion,
and unattached like the wind in a net—
Like a lotus unstained by water,
the leader of others, not to be led by another— him the wise call a sage.
He who stands firm amidst the flood like a pillar,
against whom others speak words beyond measure—
he is free from passion, his faculties perfectly composed.
The wise sages know that as well:
he who is firm in self, as straight as a shuttle,
loathes evil deeds.
Investigating both the uneven and the even,
the wise ones, the sages, understand that;
he who has restrained himself does no evil.
The sage who is self-restrained, whether young or middle-aged,
is beyond reproach and does not provoke anyone;
the wise indeed recognize him as a sage.
Whether at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end,
if one who lives on what is given by others should receive alms,
he is not fit for praise nor for disparagement.
The wise sages know that very thing:
the sage who wanders, having abstained from sexual intercourse,
and who in his youth is not bound to anything at all.
The wise call him a sage who has abandoned negligence, is free from intoxication,
and has understood the world as one who sees the ultimate truth.
Having crossed over the ocean of the flood,
such a one is free from bonds, unattached,
and taintless; the wise call him a sage.
Unequal are these two who dwell far apart:
the householder who supports a wife and the virtuous one who is free from possessiveness.
The unrestrained householder lives for the sake of obstructing the life of others.
The sage, being restrained, constantly protects living beings.
Just as a blue-necked peacock cannot ever attain the speed of a swan,
so too [the world] cannot reach the pace of the Sage.
Thus the householder does not emulate the monk,
the sage who meditates in solitude within the forest.
Thus ends the twelfth discourse, the Munisutta.
The First Chapter: The Chapter on Snakes.
Its summary verse:
The Snake and Dhaniya, indeed...
The horn and likewise the ploughing;
Cunda, ruin, and the outcaste, and the cultivation of loving-kindness.
Sātāgira, Āḷavaka,
and likewise the sage Vijaya—
these are the twelve discourses.
It is called the Uragavagga (The Chapter on Snakes).
